introduction: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, treats the fragile peace of Edward IV's court as an opportunity to turn suspicion, family rivalry and public ceremony towards his own advancement. He shares his schemes with the audience while presenting loyalty and humility to those he means to use. Around him, bereaved women recall the violence that made the present dynasty, children inherit dangerous claims, and powerful allies weigh advantage against conscience. The succession becomes a contest over who can command belief as well as obedience.

fullSynopsis.text: In the peace established under his brother Edward IV, Richard, Duke of Gloucester, announces his intention to pursue villainy. He has turned Edward against their brother Clarence through a prophecy about a murderer identified by the letter G. As Clarence is taken to the Tower, Richard professes affection while planning his death and blaming Queen Elizabeth's family. He also courts Lady Anne beside Henry VI's corpse, although he killed both Henry and her husband. Through calculated self-abasement and claims of love, he persuades her to accept his ring and consider him more favourably.

The court is divided between Elizabeth's relatives and their enemies. The displaced Queen Margaret recalls the destruction of her own family and curses those who profited by it, warning Buckingham especially against Richard. Richard sends two murderers to Clarence. Haunted by a dream of drowning and judgement for his past crimes, Clarence still trusts his brother until the killers reveal their commission. His pleas stir one man's conscience, but the other stabs him and carries him away to drown in wine. Edward attempts to reconcile the rival factions, then learns that Clarence is dead despite his countermand and is overwhelmed by remorse.

Edward dies, leaving the young Prince Edward to succeed him. Richard and Buckingham arrange to bring the prince from Ludlow with a small escort, then arrest Rivers, Grey and Vaughan, separating him from his mother's supporters. Elizabeth takes her younger son York into sanctuary. Citizens fear the contest for power around a child king. Buckingham persuades the Cardinal to obtain York from sanctuary, and the brothers are lodged in the Tower. Catesby finds that Hastings, though pleased by the approaching deaths of Elizabeth's allies, will not support Richard's accession at the princes' expense.

Rivers, Grey and Vaughan go to execution at Pomfret. Hastings ignores Stanley's warning and attends a council supposedly preparing the coronation. Richard invents an accusation of witchcraft involving Elizabeth and Mistress Shore, calls Hastings a traitor and orders his immediate beheading. He and Buckingham present the death to London's mayor as the suppression of a plot. A scrivener observes that Hastings's indictment was prepared before his alleged offence. Buckingham then attacks the legitimacy of Edward's family, but the citizens respond with silence. Richard nevertheless stages pious reluctance before the mayor and accepts the crown as if yielding to public demand.

Richard's rise leaves the princes' mother, grandmother and Anne unable even to visit them. Anne, now Richard's wife, dreads her coronation and describes her miserable marriage. Elizabeth sends Dorset to join Richmond abroad. Once crowned, Richard demands the princes' deaths. Buckingham's hesitation costs him Richard's trust, and his claim to a promised reward is dismissed; he flees and later rebels. Richard employs Tyrrel, who reports that Dighton and Forrest have smothered the boys. Richard confines Clarence's son, marries Clarence's daughter beneath her rank, and reports Anne's death. He now seeks his niece Elizabeth's hand to thwart Richmond's rival marriage claim.

Margaret, Elizabeth and the Duchess of York measure their losses against one another. Richard's mother curses him before battle, and Elizabeth confronts him with her murdered children. Richard presses her to persuade her daughter to marry him; she leaves promising to report the daughter's answer, which he interprets as success. Stanley subsequently tells Richmond's messenger that Elizabeth has agreed to Richmond's marriage instead. Richard's enemies gather, though floods disperse Buckingham's army and he is captured. Stanley secretly supports Richmond but fears for his son George, whom Richard holds hostage. Buckingham is led to execution, acknowledging his broken oaths and Margaret's warning.

The armies meet at Bosworth. During the night, ghosts of Richard's victims condemn him and encourage Richmond. Richard wakes terrified by conscience and isolation, then tries to dismiss the dreams and rally his men. Stanley refuses to bring his forces; Richard orders George killed, but the battle delays the execution. Unhorsed, Richard fights on in search of Richmond. They meet in combat, and Richmond kills him. Stanley brings the crown to the victor and confirms George's safety. Richmond offers pardon to returning fugitives and announces his intended marriage to Elizabeth, presenting the union of Lancaster and York as the end of England's civil bloodshed.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Richard presents his own exclusion from courtly pleasure as a reason to pursue villainy and reveals the plot that has sent Clarence to the Tower. He pretends brotherly concern and blames Elizabeth's relatives. Meeting Anne with Henry VI's funeral procession, he turns her denunciation of his killings into a courtship and secures her acceptance of a ring. At court, Richard aggravates factional hostility while denying that he practises deceit. Margaret interrupts with accusations and curses rooted in the earlier wars, warning Buckingham not to trust him. Richard commissions Clarence's murder. In the Tower, Clarence recounts a terrifying dream and appeals to conscience, family and divine law, but one murderer kills him while the other repents.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: The dying Edward reconciles his courtiers in a formal exchange of promises. Richard performs goodwill, then announces Clarence's death, claiming the countermand arrived too late. Edward remembers his brother's services and condemns the failure of others and himself to intercede. After Edward's death, Elizabeth, Clarence's children and the Duchess of York mourn their overlapping losses. Buckingham proposes that Prince Edward come from Ludlow with only a small train; privately he and Richard plan to detach him from his mother's family. Citizens discuss the dangers of minority rule and competing uncles. News arrives that Rivers, Grey and Vaughan have been imprisoned by Richard and Buckingham, and Elizabeth takes York into sanctuary.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: The prince reaches London without his arrested maternal supporters. Buckingham overrides the Cardinal's scruples about sanctuary, and York is brought to join his brother in the Tower. Hastings refuses Catesby's suggestion that Richard should be king, yet dismisses Stanley's warning and rejoices in his enemies' impending deaths. Rivers, Grey and Vaughan are led to execution. Richard uses a fabricated witchcraft accusation to condemn Hastings at the coronation council, then supplies the mayor with a false account of treason. The scrivener exposes the indictment's advance preparation. Buckingham's public campaign gains little response, but he and Richard stage a pious, reluctant acceptance of the crown before the mayor and citizens.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: The women are denied access to the princes, and Anne reluctantly leaves to be crowned Richard's queen. Elizabeth sends Dorset to Richmond. Richard's demand for the princes' murder unsettles Buckingham; after Richard withholds his promised reward, Buckingham flees. Tyrrel arranges the boys' suffocation and reports it to Richard, who also reports Anne's death and seeks his niece Elizabeth in marriage. Margaret joins the grieving women before Richard's mother curses him. Elizabeth rebuts his marriage arguments but leaves him expecting cooperation; Stanley later reports her consent to Richmond's rival match. Rebellions spread, Buckingham's army disperses in floods, and he is captured. Richard holds Stanley's son hostage while preparing to confront Richmond.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Buckingham goes to execution, recognizing the return upon himself of his false oaths and Margaret's warning. Richmond advances against Richard, and both prepare their forces at Bosworth. Stanley visits Richmond secretly but cannot openly commit himself while his son remains Richard's hostage. Ghosts of Richard's victims appear to both leaders: they promise Richard defeat and Richmond victory. Richard wakes terrified, then attempts to reject conscience and dreams. Stanley withholds his army, and Richard's order to kill George is postponed. Richard fights fiercely after losing his horse, but Richmond kills him in combat. With George safe and the crown recovered, Richmond proposes marriage to Elizabeth and the reconciliation of the rival houses.
